questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a correlation length measures in a chain
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a correlation length measures in a flexible chain
questions.stem: A note describes a chain in which distant links lose their alignment. Explain in writing what a correlation length measures in such a chain.

answer.exemplar: The correlation length is the distance over which the local orientation of one segment remains correlated with that of another, so beyond it the alignment has been lost to random thermal motion. A short correlation length means the chain is locally disordered and flexible, while a long one means stiff segments that stay aligned over many segments. It measures a structural length in space, not a time and not the overall size of the chain.

questions.explanation: It measures local stiffness, not the overall chain size and not any timescale, which is why it is a length at all.
questions.hint: It measures how far alignment persists.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a solid's heat capacity falls at low temperature
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the heat capacity of a solid falls as the temperature drops
questions.stem: A note describes a solid specimen that behaves normally at room temperature but stiffens when cooled. Explain in writing why the heat capacity of a solid falls as the temperature drops.

answer.exemplar: A solid stores thermal energy in the vibrational modes of its lattice, and each mode can only accept energy in steps set by its quantum spacing. As the temperature falls, fewer and fewer modes have spacing small enough to be populated, so the heat capacity drops steeply, following a cubic law at the lowest temperatures before the exponential regime at the very bottom. The classical argument in which every mode contributes equally is then no longer valid, which is why the measured curve turns down sharply.

questions.explanation: The classical count of modes, which gives a constant heat capacity, simply breaks down at low temperature.
questions.hint: Modes must be excited before they can store energy.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a junction leaves a charge-free region
questions.learningObjective: Explain the origin and role of the charge-free region at a junction
questions.stem: A device note states that a region near the junction interface carries essentially no mobile charge. Explain in writing how such a charge-free region arises and what it does.

answer.exemplar: When two differently doped materials are joined, the concentration gradient pushes electrons and holes across the interface, leaving behind fixed ionised donor and acceptor atoms. These fixed charges create a barrier field that opposes further diffusion, so diffusion stops once the field balances the gradient and the region contains only the immobile ionised atoms. The region supports the built-in voltage, and widening it as the reverse bias grows is what gives the device its blocking behaviour.

questions.explanation: Its width and the built-in voltage it supports are what set the blocking behaviour of the device.
questions.hint: Diffusion leaves fixed ions behind.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Distinguishing ductile from brittle behaviour
questions.learningObjective: Separate ductile from brittle behaviour using strain at failure and absorbed energy
questions.stem: A note compares two implants, one that bent before it broke and one that snapped. Explain in writing how to tell ductile behaviour from brittle behaviour using measured quantities.

answer.exemplar: Ductile and brittle behaviour differ in how much permanent deformation a material absorbs before it fails, and that difference shows up in several measured quantities. A ductile specimen shows a yield stress, after which the stress continues to rise only slowly as the strain grows a great deal, and it absorbs a large amount of energy before cracking. A brittle specimen shows almost no plastic strain and fails at a stress close to its fracture stress, often without any obvious warning, and absorbs much less energy. Measurements of strain at failure and of the area under the stress-strain curve therefore separate the two behaviours directly.

questions.explanation: Measuring strain at failure and the area under the stress-strain curve separates the two behaviours directly.
questions.hint: Look at plastic strain and absorbed energy.

questions.stem: A note records that a chain's segments stay aligned over a distance of 0.5 nm but lose alignment beyond that. Explain in writing how this number connects to the bending stiffness of the material.

answer.exemplar: The correlation length measures how far the orientation of neighbouring segments stays correlated, and it is set by the competition between the bending stiffness, which resists changes of direction, and the random thermal agitation that tends to destroy the alignment. A stiff material has a large bending rigidity, so thermal fluctuations bend it only slightly over a given length and the alignment survives further, giving a longer correlation length. answer.exemplar: A heat capacity close to absolute zero measures how many vibrational modes of the solid can be excited at that low temperature, and only the very softest, longest-wavelength modes qualify. answer.exemplar: The width of the depleted region follows from the balance between the fixed space charge of the dopants and the field that the applied bias sets up across the junction, and the dopant density and the built-in potential both appear in that balance. questions.explanation: Because the built-in potential varies with temperature, the width shifts and can be calibrated into a thermometer.
questions.hint: Doping and bias set the width; temperature shifts it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Distinguishing ductile from brittle behaviour
questions.learningObjective: Explain why materials of the same composition can differ in ductility
questions.stem: A note records two specimens with the same composition, one failing at a low strain and one deforming a long way before cracking. Explain in writing why the same composition can give such different behaviour.

answer.exemplar: Composition sets the bonding, but the observed failure behaviour also depends on how the material is processed and on its microstructure. Grain size, the presence of defects or precipitates, and the temperature all change how easily dislocations move, and that mobility is what separates ductile deformation from sudden brittle cracking. A specimen with mobile dislocations spreads its strain over a large volume before a crack runs, whereas one with locked or sharp defects concentrates stress and cracks with almost no plastic strain. The chemistry can therefore be identical while the mechanical response differs widely.

questions.explanation: That mobility, not the chemistry alone, is what separates ductile deformation from sudden brittle cracking.
questions.hint: Microstructure decides whether dislocations move.

answer.exemplar: The correlation length records how far the orientation of one segment of the chain stays aligned with a neighbouring segment before thermal motion destroys the correlation.
